shots.text: At Pangwari, excavated between 2011 and 2014, they found a terracotta deposit in a secure archaeological context for the first time.
shots.desc: generic close-up of a trowel cleaning red soil, no finds visible

shots.text: The team interprets some deposits as graves, marked by upright stones in a row; no human remains survive.
shots.desc: a row of plain upright field stones in grassland at dusk, no finds, no people

shots.text: So what kind of society was this?
shots.desc: dusk over a dispersed farming landscape

shots.text: Breunig and Rupp concluded that Nok developed complexity only in terms of ritual.
shots.desc: a row of upright stones at night, low firelight

shots.text: They describe small groups of farmers, living autonomously in dispersed settlements.
shots.desc: a few homesteads spaced far apart across fields, morning

shots.text: The excavators found no evidence of a state or an elite.
shots.desc: open hilltop, no structures, wind in grass

shots.text: That is not proof of absence: they stress that preservation is poor, and the data come from a limited area.
shots.desc: acidic red soil, roots, a single sherd

shots.text: There might have been rulers or chiefs, they write, who left no status markers.
shots.desc: footprints fading on a dirt track

shots.text: But on the evidence so far, Breunig says, highly accomplished art does not necessarily require a complex society.
shots.credit: Nok kneeling figure · Honolulu Museum of Art (8348.1) · Photo: Hiart, CC0

shots.desc: overgrown trench, weeds, collapsed string lines
